A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PULSE framework and OpenHands study. All 20 pages of each version, including Appendices A–D, are readable and support comparison. Renumbered and relocated material can be matched.

before.justification: V1 reports original user-satisfaction experiments across approximately 36k sessions and 15k users, prediction-model evaluations, benchmark comparisons, and memory-management simulations.

after.justification: V3 retains these original results and adds feedback-validity analyses, automatic feature-discovery evaluations, conversation costs, and predictor-dependent confidence-interval reductions.

M1.justification: The operative PULSE pipeline retains work-segment ratings, the same 15 features, prediction models, and PPI effect estimation. V3 documents feature selection and explores automatic feature rediscovery, but does not report replacing the features or procedure used in the deployed experiments.

E1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds an auxiliary evaluation task: generating reusable satisfaction-feature definitions and measuring recovery of the original feature set. The deployed coding tasks, seven benchmark comparisons, and SWE-Bench memory simulations remain unchanged. Shopping, research, and travel applications in Table 12 are prospective.

E2.justification: V3 Table 11 adds LogReg and HGB variants to the downstream CI-reduction comparison previously reported using RF. Table 4 adds a feature-discovery comparison involving o3, gpt-4o, gpt-5.1, claude-opus-4.5, and claude-4-sonnet. The original satisfaction-prediction comparators remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Added analyses introduce rank-biserial comparisons across labeled and unlabeled trajectories, manual inspection of 20 low-rated sessions, and feature-recovery scoring. The original conversation-level randomization, case-study durations, sample requirements, five-fold validation, and memory-simulation settings are retained; expanded cross-validation documentation does not establish a changed protocol.

E4.justification: V3 substantially expands validation of the measurement framework: it examines feedback representativeness, relationships between ratings and git actions, failures in low-rated sessions, automatic recovery of features, and CI sensitivity to predictor family. These address several previously unexamined questions about feedback validity and dependence on modeling choices.

E5.justification: Appendix A.2 newly specifies random seed 42 for the existing five-fold procedure, without establishing additional runs. Table 10 newly reports standard deviations of conversation costs. Existing prediction-score uncertainty, effect-size confidence intervals, and significance reporting are otherwise retained.

E6.justification: The seven original numerical tables match their counterparts in v3, but substantial diagnostic results are added. These include a labeled–unlabeled message-count effect of RBC=0.32, rating–git-action correlations, feature-recovery results, conversation costs, and predictor-specific CI reductions. For Claude-3.7 versus Claude-4, Table 11 reports reductions of 3.57%, 17.55%, and 61.5% for LogReg, HGB, and RF.

T1.justification: The work-segment definitions, mean estimators, PPI effect estimator, asymptotic argument, and Wald interval remain mathematically equivalent. V3 explains existing PPI bias-correction and shared-distribution requirements, without adding a formal result, proof, or substantive derivation.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain PULSE, its large-scale software-agent deployment, stronger effects from backbone changes than scaffolding changes, approximately 40% narrower confidence intervals, and discrepancies between benchmarks and human ratings. Revised novelty wording and broader-framework emphasis develop the existing claims.

C2.justification: V3 interprets feedback-group similarity as suggesting similar experiences among silent users, connects low ratings to concrete interaction failures, and explicitly acknowledges unmodeled label noise. Table 12 develops prospective applications beyond coding. These extend interpretation and qualifications while retaining the single-platform limitation.

D1.justification: V3 documents expert-assisted feature selection, the automatic-discovery prompt and JSONL workflow, and pooled out-of-fold evaluation. Original model hyperparameters remain unchanged. V1 supplies a repository link; v3 omits it and promises code plus anonymized feature-level datasets. The PDFs do not establish actual release availability.

R1.justification: V3 adds literature grounding for implicit feedback, dialogue failures, and task-progression features, alongside product citations and a comparison of evaluation paradigms in Table 1. The main positioning remains stable. The updated Ambig-SWE title and publication reference identify the previously cited work.

P1.justification: V3 substantially reorganizes the narrative: related work moves before methods, deployment becomes a separate section, and results are divided into agent-design effects and evaluation efficiency. Prediction-model results move out of methods. The introduction, related work, methodological explanations, and conclusion are extensively revised, and an impact statement is added.

P2.justification: The main text and references switch from one to two columns, with extensive resizing and redistribution of displays. V3 adds a main-text feedback screenshot and five tables covering positioning, feature discovery, costs, CI reductions, and prospective applications. Existing figures are retained with presentation adjustments, including revised feature-difference axis labels.

improvement.justification: The added feedback-validity checks and predictor-sensitivity analysis strengthen the evidence supporting PULSE, while feature-selection and cross-validation details improve transparency. These gains outweigh localized regressions: Table 4 reports Claude totals of 12/15 although their components sum to 11/15, Section 6.2 garbles the CI explanation, and the repository link disappears. The additional checks provide useful but partial validation, supporting a modest overall improvement.
